# Purpose and assumed background {.unnumbered}

This note assumes only basic calculus, familiar PMFs and PDFs, and the
definition of a measure from
[Measure and probability foundations](measure-probability-foundations.qmd).
It does not assume real analysis.

The goals are to explain precisely:

- what **Lebesgue measure** is;
- what $dx$ means in a measure integral;
- why a density value is not a point probability;
- how one integral covers discrete, continuous, and mixed distributions;
- what $P\ll\nu$ and $dP/d\nu$ mean.

# 1. Lebesgue measure is the usual notion of length

Lebesgue measure on the real line is denoted by $\lambda$. Its basic defining
behavior is

$$
\lambda((a,b))=b-a.
$$

The choice of open, closed, or half-open endpoints does not affect length:

$$
\lambda((a,b))
=\lambda([a,b])
=\lambda((a,b])
=b-a.
$$

Lebesgue measure extends ordinary interval length to a large collection of more
complicated subsets of $\mathbb R$ while preserving countable additivity.

It is helpful to think of $\lambda$ as a standardized ruler:

| Set | Lebesgue measure |
|---|---:|
| $(2,5)$ | 3 |
| $(0,1)\cup(3,5)$ | 3 |
| $\{7\}$ | 0 |
| Any finite set | 0 |
| Any countable set | 0 |
| $\mathbb R$ | $\infty$ |

Lebesgue measure is a measure, but it is not a probability measure on all of
$\mathbb R$, because $\lambda(\mathbb R)=\infty$ rather than 1.

## Why a point has length zero

For every $\varepsilon>0$, the point $a$ lies inside

$$
\left(a-\frac\varepsilon2,a+\frac\varepsilon2\right),
$$

an interval of length $\varepsilon$. The only nonnegative length no greater
than every positive $\varepsilon$ is zero. Thus

$$
\lambda(\{a\})=0.
$$

By countable additivity, any countable collection of points also has Lebesgue
measure zero.

This does **not** mean countable sets are empty. “Measure zero” means they take
up no length according to $\lambda$.

# 2. The subsets that receive Lebesgue length

Lebesgue measure is defined on a sigma-field of **Lebesgue-measurable sets**.
This collection includes all intervals, all open and closed sets, all countable
sets, and all sets obtained from these through countable unions,
intersections, and complements.

The **Borel sigma-field** is

$$
\mathcal B(\mathbb R)=\sigma\{(a,b):a<b\}.
$$

Here $\sigma\{(a,b):a<b\}$ means:

> the smallest sigma-field containing every open interval.

The word “smallest” means the intersection of all sigma-fields that contain
those intervals. You do not need to construct its members one at a time.

Every Borel set is Lebesgue measurable. The Lebesgue sigma-field additionally
contains subsets of Borel sets having Lebesgue measure zero. Most probability
and statistical work on $\mathbb R$ uses Borel sets and does not require
tracking this distinction explicitly.

# 3. Restricting length creates a probability distribution

Define

$$
P(A)=\lambda\{A\cap(0,1)\}.
\tag{1}
$$

Equation (1) measures how much of $A$ lies inside $(0,1)$. Because that
interval has length one,

$$
P(\mathbb R)=\lambda((0,1))=1.
$$

Therefore $P$ is a probability measure: the Uniform$(0,1)$ distribution.

For example,

$$
P\{(0.2,0.5)\}=0.3,
\qquad
P(\{0.4\})=0.
$$

# 4. Integration with respect to a measure

The notation

$$
\int h(x)\,\mu(dx)
$$

means “integrate the function $h$ using the sizes supplied by $\mu$.” The
measure tells the integral how much weight different regions receive.

## Start with an indicator

For an indicator function,

$$
\boxed{
\int\mathbf 1_A(x)\,\mu(dx)=\mu(A).
}
\tag{2}
$$

This is the fundamental connection between measuring sets and integrating
functions.

## Then use a step function

Suppose $A_1,\ldots,A_K$ are disjoint and

$$
s(x)=\sum_{k=1}^Kc_k\mathbf 1_{A_k}(x),
\qquad c_k\geq0.
$$

Then define

$$
\int s(x)\mu(dx)
=\sum_{k=1}^Kc_k\mu(A_k).
\tag{3}
$$

The integral is a weighted sum of the heights $c_k$, where the measure of each
region supplies its weight.

General nonnegative measurable functions are approximated from below by such
step functions. A function that can be negative is separated into
$h^+(x)=\max\{h(x),0\}$ and $h^-(x)=\max\{-h(x),0\}$, so that
$h=h^+-h^-$. You do not need the construction proof to use the integral, but
equations (2) and (3) explain what is being generalized.

# 5. How this relates to the calculus integral

When the integrating measure is Lebesgue measure,

$$
\int h(x)\,\lambda(dx)
$$

is normally abbreviated as

$$
\int h(x)\,dx.
$$

Thus the $dx$ in an ordinary continuous probability calculation can be read
as “integrate with respect to length.”

For well-behaved functions, the Riemann and Lebesgue integrals have the same
value. Their constructions emphasize different things:

- a Riemann sum partitions the input axis into small intervals;
- a Lebesgue integral begins from the measure of sets and extends (3).

Lebesgue integration handles limits and irregular functions more reliably,
which is why modern probability uses it.

# 6. A continuous density is relative to Lebesgue measure

Suppose $p(x)\geq0$ and

$$
\int_{\mathbb R}p(x)\,dx=1.
$$

Define a probability measure by

$$
\boxed{
P(A)=\int_Ap(x)\,\lambda(dx)=\int_Ap(x)\,dx.
}
\tag{4}
$$

Then $p$ is the density of $P$ **relative to Lebesgue measure**.

The compact measure identity

$$
P(dx)=p(x)\lambda(dx)
\tag{5}
$$

means exactly that (4) holds for every measurable set $A$. It is not a claim
that an infinitesimal set called $dx$ exists.

## Density height is not point probability

For a continuous distribution,

$$
P(\{x\})=0
$$

even if $p(x)>0$ or $p(x)>1$. Probability comes from area over a set:

$$
P(a<X\leq b)=\int_a^bp(x)\,dx.
$$

For small positive $\Delta$ and a continuous density,

$$
P(x<X\leq x+\Delta)\approx p(x)\Delta.
$$

This approximation can motivate a density, but the exact object is (4), not a
point probability $p(x)dx$.

# 7. Counting measure makes a PMF a density

For a countable set $\mathcal X$, define **counting measure** $\#$ by

$$
\#(A)=\text{number of points in }A,
$$

allowing the value $\infty$.

If $p(x)$ is a PMF, then

$$
P(A)=\sum_{x\in A}p(x)
=\int_Ap(x)\,\#(dx).
\tag{6}
$$

Thus a PMF and a PDF are both densities. They differ in their reference
measures:

| Statistical object | Reference measure | Integral |
|---|---|---|
| PMF $p$ | Counting measure $\#$ | $\sum_xp(x)$ |
| Continuous PDF $p$ | Lebesgue measure $\lambda$ | $\int p(x)dx$ |

This is why the phrase “the density” is incomplete unless the reference
measure is understood.

# 8. Dirac measure represents a point mass

The Dirac measure at $a$ is

$$
\delta_a(A)=\mathbf 1(a\in A).
$$

It gives the point $a$ probability one. Consequently,

$$
\int h(x)\delta_a(dx)=h(a).
$$

It has no density relative to Lebesgue measure because

$$
\lambda(\{a\})=0
\quad\text{but}\quad
\delta_a(\{a\})=1.
$$

The dedicated [Dirac note](dirac-measure-and-dirac-delta.qmd) explains the
difference between this measure and the generalized “delta function.”

# 9. Null sets, almost everywhere, and almost surely

A set $N$ is **$\mu$-null** if $\mu(N)=0$.

A statement holds **$\mu$-almost everywhere**, abbreviated $\mu$-a.e., if it
may fail on a $\mu$-null set but holds everywhere else.

For example, the two functions

$$
f(x)=0
$$

and

$$
g(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{0\}}(x)
$$

are equal Lebesgue-almost everywhere. They differ at $0$, but $\{0\}$ has
Lebesgue measure zero. Therefore their Lebesgue integrals are identical.

When the relevant measure is a probability measure $P$, “$P$-almost
everywhere” is usually called **$P$-almost surely**, abbreviated $P$-a.s.

Thus

$$
Y_n\to Y\quad P\text{-almost surely}
$$

means convergence for every elementary outcome except possibly outcomes in an
event having probability zero.

Probability zero does not mean logically impossible. For a Uniform$(0,1)$
variable, every particular point has probability zero, but some value must be
observed.

# 10. Absolute continuity is a relationship between measures

Let $P$ and $\nu$ be measures on the same measurable space. We say that $P$ is
**absolutely continuous with respect to** $\nu$, written

$$
P\ll\nu,
$$

if

$$
\boxed{
\nu(A)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad P(A)=0
}
\tag{7}
$$

for every measurable $A$.

Plain-language reading:

> $P$ does not place positive mass on any set that $\nu$ considers negligible.

Examples:

- A normal distribution is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue
  measure.
- A discrete distribution is absolutely continuous with respect to counting
  measure.
- $\delta_a$ is not absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure.

The direction matters. For example, a Uniform$(0,1)$ probability measure is
absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, but Lebesgue measure on
all of $\mathbb R$ is not absolutely continuous with respect to that uniform
law: the set $(2,3)$ has uniform probability zero but Lebesgue measure one.

# 11. The Radon-Nikodym derivative is a measure-level density

The Radon-Nikodym theorem says, under conditions satisfied by the standard
probability models and reference measures used in these notes, that if
$P\ll\nu$, then there is a measurable function $p$ such that

$$
P(A)=\int_Ap\,d\nu
\quad\text{for every measurable }A.
\tag{8}
$$

That function is written

$$
\boxed{
p=\frac{dP}{d\nu}
}
\tag{9}
$$

and is called the **Radon-Nikodym derivative** of $P$ with respect to $\nu$.

A common sufficient condition is that the measures be **sigma-finite**.
Sigma-finite means that the whole space can be covered by countably many
measurable sets, each having finite measure. Probability measures are finite
and hence sigma-finite. Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ is sigma-finite because
$\mathbb R=\bigcup_{m=1}^{\infty}[-m,m]$, and each interval has finite length.
Counting measure on a countable space is also sigma-finite. These are the
reference measures used in the examples here.

You do not need the proof for Walker. Operationally, (9) means that $p$ is the
weighting function that converts integration under $\nu$ into integration
under $P$, for every suitable integrand $h$:

$$
\int h\,dP
=\int h\frac{dP}{d\nu}\,d\nu.
\tag{10}
$$

Equation (9) generalizes both PDFs and PMFs:

$$
\text{PDF}=\frac{dP}{d\lambda},
\qquad
\text{PMF}=\frac{dP}{d\#}.
$$

The derivative is unique only up to $\nu$-null sets. Changing its value at one
Lebesgue-null point does not change the probability measure.

# 12. Dominating measures

If every distribution $P_\theta$ in a statistical model satisfies

$$
P_\theta\ll\nu,
$$

then $\nu$ is a **common dominating measure**. Each model distribution has a
density

$$
p_\theta=\frac{dP_\theta}{d\nu}.
$$

The familiar likelihood

$$
L(\theta;x)=p_\theta(x)
$$

is a density value relative to this shared reference measure. Common choices
are Lebesgue measure for continuous models and counting measure for discrete
models.

# 13. Mixed distributions also fit the framework

Consider

$$
P=0.2\delta_0+0.8\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1).
$$

This distribution has a point mass at zero and a continuous component. It has
no density relative to Lebesgue measure alone because of the atom.

An **atom** is a point receiving positive probability; here
$P(\{0\})=0.2$.

Choose instead

$$
\nu=\delta_0+\lambda.
$$

Then $P\ll\nu$ and one version of its density is

$$
\frac{dP}{d\nu}(x)
=0.2\mathbf 1_{\{0\}}(x)
+0.8\mathbf 1_{(0,1)}(x).
$$

For any measurable $A$,

$$
\int_A\frac{dP}{d\nu}\,d\nu
=0.2\mathbf 1(0\in A)
+0.8\lambda\{A\cap(0,1)\}.
$$

This example shows why measure notation is more general than the artificial
choice between “PMF” and “PDF.”

# 14. Expectation is integration under a probability measure

If $X$ has distribution $P_X$, then

$$
E\{h(X)\}=\int h(x)P_X(dx).
$$

This becomes

$$
\sum_xh(x)p(x)
$$

in the discrete case and

$$
\int h(x)p(x)dx
$$

in the continuous case. These are not two unrelated definitions; they are two
forms of the same measure integral.

# 15. When two integrals appear

Bayesian nonparametrics often contains an integral over data values inside an
integral over possible distributions. For example,

$$
\int_{\mathcal D}
\left\{\int_{\mathcal X}h(x,f)P_f(dx)\right\}\Pi(df).
$$

Changing the order of integration is not merely typographical. Tonelli's
theorem permits it for nonnegative measurable $h$; Fubini's theorem permits it
when the absolute integral is finite. Later notes say “under conditions that
permit exchanging the order” rather than proving these theorems.

# A compact dictionary

| Notation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\lambda$ | Lebesgue length measure |
| $dx$ | Usually shorthand for $\lambda(dx)$ |
| $\#$ | Counting measure |
| $P(dx)$ | Integrate with respect to probability measure $P$ |
| $P(dx)=p(x)\nu(dx)$ | $p$ is a density of $P$ relative to $\nu$ |
| $P\ll\nu$ | Every $\nu$-null set is also $P$-null |
| $dP/d\nu$ | Radon-Nikodym density of $P$ relative to $\nu$ |
| $\mu$-a.e. | Except possibly on a set having $\mu$-measure zero |
| $P$-a.s. | Except possibly on an event having probability zero |
| dominating measure | One reference measure relative to which all model distributions have densities |

# Check your understanding

Select each **Answer** box after working out the question yourself.

**1. What is $\lambda((2,7))$? What is $\lambda(\{2\})$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Lebesgue measure agrees with ordinary interval length, so
$\lambda((2,7))=7-2=5$. A singleton has zero length, so
$\lambda(\{2\})=0$.
:::

**2. Why can $p(2)>0$ while $P(\{2\})=0$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

$p(2)$ is a density **height**, not probability mass at the point 2. For a
Lebesgue density,

$$
P(\{2\})=\int_{\{2\}}p(x)\,\lambda(dx)=0
$$

because the singleton has Lebesgue measure zero, even if $p(2)$ is positive or
very large.
:::

**3. With respect to which measure is a PMF a density?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Counting measure on the discrete support. Integration against counting measure
is summation, so $P(A)=\sum_{x\in A}p(x)$.
:::

**4. Translate $P\ll\nu$ into a sentence about null sets.**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

$P$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $\nu$: every $\nu$-null set is
also $P$-null. In symbols, $\nu(A)=0$ implies $P(A)=0$ for every measurable
$A$.
:::

**5. Why is $\delta_0\not\ll\lambda$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Take $A=\{0\}$. Lebesgue measure gives $\lambda(A)=0$, but the Dirac measure
gives $\delta_0(A)=1$. Thus a $\lambda$-null set need not be $\delta_0$-null,
which violates the definition of $\delta_0\ll\lambda$.
:::

**6. What equation defines $dP/d\nu$ operationally?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The Radon--Nikodym derivative $p=dP/d\nu$ is the function satisfying

$$
P(A)=\int_A p\,d\nu
$$

for every measurable set $A$. This integral identity—not an infinitesimal
quotient—is its operational meaning.
:::

**7. What is the difference between “almost surely” and “surely for every
possible outcome”?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

“Almost surely” allows exceptions, but the set of exceptional outcomes must
have probability zero. “For every possible outcome” allows no exceptions at
all. A probability-zero outcome can still belong to the sample space, so the
two statements are not logically identical.
:::
